procedural_history.originating_court: Not explicitly stated, but the case involves an occurrence dated February 4, 1965, suggesting a trial court in Madhya Pradesh initially heard the matter.
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated February 27, 1967, of the Madhya Pradesh High Court, Indore Bench in Criminal Appeals Nos. 238 and 249 of 1965.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Two criminal appeals were before the High Court, filed by two rival factions. Both sides repeated their plea of self-defense, which was rejected by the High Court.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants approached the Supreme Court by special leave, challenging the High Court's judgment. There are two appeals before the Supreme Court: Criminal Appeal No. 83 of 1968 and Criminal Appeal No. 204 of 1967.

decision.appeal_result: Cr. A. No, 204 of 1967 allowed. Cr. A. No. 83 of 1968 dismissed. Criminal Appeal No. 83 of 1968 must, therefore, fail and the same is hereby dismissed.

issue.issue_text: Whether the inhabitants of village JS were justified in using force in self-defence against the inhabitants of village NS, who were armed with dangerous weapons and waiting for them, while the former were lawfully exercising their right to return from the Mosque to their village.

facts: The inhabitants of two villages, JS and NS, were hostile towards each other.
The only route for the people of village JS to reach the Sanwar Mosque for Id prayers passed through village NS.
On the day of the incident, after prayers, the inhabitants of NS returned to their village first, armed themselves with dangerous weapons, and waited on the road for the JS inhabitants to return.
When the JS inhabitants were returning to their village along this route, they were confronted by the armed group from NS.
law: A person cannot be deprived of their right to use a lawful route simply because it passes through an area inhabited by people who are hostile towards them.
The right of private defence is available to a person who is lawfully exercising their rights and is confronted with unlawful aggression.
The law on self-defence (ss. 96 to 106 of the Indian Penal Code) is intended to encourage a spirit of self-defence against grave danger and does not require a law-abiding citizen to act cowardly.
The party that initiates the aggression (the aggressor) is not entitled to claim the right of private defence.
application: The Court determined that the people of village JS were lawfully exercising their right to travel back to their village from the mosque using the only available route.

The Court identified the inhabitants of village NS as the aggressors. This was because they had returned from the mosque early, deliberately armed themselves, and positioned themselves on the road specifically to wait for and confront the JS villagers.
Since the JS villagers were acting lawfully and were met with unlawful aggression from the armed NS group, they were fully justified in using force to defend themselves.
Conversely, because the NS villagers were the aggressors, they had no right of private defence against the actions of the JS villagers.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the inhabitants of village JS were justified in using force in self-defence because they were lawfully exercising their right to return home when they were confronted by the inhabitants of village NS, who were the aggressors, having armed themselves and waited for the confrontation.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was correct in its observation that the trial court had erroneously acquitted some members of the unlawful assemblies for offences under Section 302, read with Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code, as they were all liable pursuant to the common object of the assembly.

facts: The High Court, while reviewing the case, made an observation that the trial court had made a mistake.
The mistake, according to the High Court, was acquitting some members of the unlawful assemblies of murder charges (Section 302 IPC).
The High Court believed that based on Section 149 of the IPC, all members were vicariously liable for the murder because it was committed in pursuit of the assembly's common object.
law: An appellate court cannot overturn a verdict of acquittal and convict an accused person unless the state has specifically filed an appeal against that acquittal.
application: In this case, the state had not filed any appeal against the trial court's decision to acquit those specific members.
Without an appeal against the acquittal, the High Court had no legal authority to change the trial court's verdict for those individuals.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the High Court's observation because, despite its opinion on the matter, the High Court was legally powerless to act on it. Since there was no appeal against the acquittal, the High Court could do nothing more than make a comment, and its observation had no legal effect on the acquitted persons.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the inhabitants of village JS were justified in using force in self-defence against the inhabitants of village NS, who were armed with dangerous weapons and waiting for them, while the former were lawfully exercising their right to return from the Mosque to their village.
appellant_arguments: The right of private defence was fully established, as they only used their weapons after two members of their group (Majid and Yasin) had already been killed.
The inhabitants of Naya Siloda were the aggressors, as they had returned to their village earlier, collected arms, and lay in wait for the Juna Siloda people.
The Juna Siloda people were entitled to protect themselves against the aggressive assault, especially since two of their unarmed men were injured when they got down from their cart.

Evidence from Naya Siloda's own witnesses supported the plea of private defence, showing that a member of the Naya Siloda group (Latif Khan) fired a gun first and was only attacked by the Juna Siloda people after he had used his weapon against them and exhausted his ammunition.
respondent_arguments: The High Court had observed that the Juna Siloda people knew the only route was through Naya Siloda and should have avoided the cart track, implying they were seeking a confrontation.
In the High Court, the plea of self-defence from both sides had been negatived.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was correct in its observation that the trial court had erroneously acquitted some members of the unlawful assemblies for offences under Section 302, read with Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code, as they were all liable pursuant to the common object of the assembly.
appellant_arguments: The text does not contain any specific arguments from the appellants on this issue. Their position would implicitly be that the trial court's acquittals were correct and the High Court's observation was wrong.
respondent_arguments: The High Court's observation, which the respondent (State) would support, was that the trial court had erroneously acquitted some members of the unlawful assemblies.
By virtue of Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code, all members of the assembly were liable for the offence of murder as it was committed in pursuance of the common object of the assembly.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When a person is in the lawful and bona fide exercise of a right, such as using a public route, they are justified in using force in self-defense if confronted by unlawful aggression, and they are not deprived of this right merely because the route passes through a hostile area.
obiter: The legislature, in enacting sections 96 to 106 of the Indian Penal Code, intended to arouse and encourage a spirit of self-defence amongst citizens when faced with grave danger.
The right of private defence is designed to serve a social purpose and deserves to be fostered within the prescribed limits.
The law does not teach cowardice, but it also does not encourage bravado.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The inhabitants of village JS were lawfully exercising their right to travel to and from the Mosque, and the fact that the only route passed through the inimical village NS did not strip them of this right. When they were confronted by the inhabitants of village NS, who were armed with dangerous weapons and waiting for them, the JS villagers were fully justified in using force to defend themselves against this unlawful aggression. The people from village NS were the aggressors and therefore had no right of private defence.
legal_tests_applied: The right of private defence under Sections 96 to 106 of the Indian Penal Code is applicable when a person, in the lawful and bona fide exercise of their rights, is confronted with unlawful aggression.

The court rejected the High Court's test that the right of self-defence is unavailable if one knowingly enters a dangerous situation, stating instead that a person is not required to abandon their lawful rights to avoid a potential confrontation.
why_appellant_lost: The appellants from village NS (in Cr. A. No. 83 of 1968) were deemed the aggressors, and as such, they had no right of private defence against the people from village JS.
why_respondent_won: The appellants from village JS (in Cr. A. No. 204 of 1967) won because they had a right to use the route from the Mosque to their village, and they were acting in the lawful and bona fide exercise of that right.
The JS villagers were confronted by the NS villagers who were armed with dangerous weapons and waiting for them, which constituted an unlawful aggression justifying the use of force in self-defence.
The High Court's approach was deemed erroneous in law, particularly its conclusion that the JS villagers should have avoided the route or that they were seeking a confrontation.
The High Court's factual finding that the JS villagers had sent their children back by another route to facilitate a confrontation was held to be without any evidence.
policy_considerations: When enacting ss. 96 to 106, I.P.C., the legislature clearly intended to arouse and encourage the manly spirit of self-defence amongst the citizens, when faced with grave danger.
The right of private defence is designed to serve a social purpose and deserves to be fostered within the prescribed limits.
The law does not require a law-abiding citizen to behave like a coward when confronted with an imminent unlawful aggression.
There is nothing more degrading to the human spirit than to run away in face of danger.
